knowledge_cards.title: Why flames look different in microgravity
knowledge_cards.text: On Earth, hot gas rises and pulls fresh air into the base of a flame, giving the familiar teardrop. In microgravity buoyancy disappears, so flames become round and blue. Oxygen then arrives only by molecular diffusion or by ventilation airflow, which makes airflow speed a key variable for spacecraft fire safety.

knowledge_cards.title: Slow airflow can lower flammability limits
knowledge_cards.text: In slow microgravity ventilation (1-10 cm/s) solid materials burn at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth (down to 13.6% O2 in BASS-II vs 18% at 1g), because gentle forced flow supplies oxygen without strong convective cooling.

knowledge_cards.title: Cool flames and reignition
knowledge_cards.text: Fuels can stop glowing visibly around 1150-1500 K yet keep reacting at 500-800 K as invisible cool flames driven by alkylperoxy chemistry (FLEX, ACME CFI-G). Unburned vapor clouds can condense and later reignite.

knowledge_cards.title: Smoke particles grow larger in microgravity
knowledge_cards.text: Without buoyant plume rise, smoke stays near its heat source longer and coagulates into larger aggregates (100-600 nm in SAME). ISS near-IR detectors missed 55% of Kapton and 66.7% of Teflon pyrolysis tests.

knowledge_cards.title: Dust baselines and false alarms (SAME + DAFT)
knowledge_cards.text: DAFT reused the SAME aerosol instruments to baseline ordinary ISS cabin dust (0.02-10+ um). Combining SAME smoke signatures with DAFT dust baselines enables polarimetric dust-discriminating smoke detectors.

knowledge_cards.title: NASA exploration atmospheres
knowledge_cards.text: NASA specifies a primary Space Exploration Atmosphere (SEA) of 8.2 psia with 34% O2, an alternate staged atmosphere of 10.2 psia with 26.5% O2, ISS air at 14.7 psia with 21% O2, and challenge reference cases at 10.2 psia with 30% O2.

knowledge_cards.title: Oxygen partial pressure comparison (pO2)
knowledge_cards.text: Oxygen partial pressure pO2 = X_O2 * P_total: ISS air = 3.09 psia; 26.5% at 10.2 psia = 2.70 psia; 34% at 8.2 psia = 2.79 psia; 30% at 10.2 psia = 3.06 psia; 4.3 psia 100% O2 EVA suit = 4.30 psia. Equal pO2 does NOT mean equal flammability because less N2 diluent reduces thermal heat capacity.

knowledge_cards.title: Partial-gravity data gap (Moon 0.165g & Mars 0.38g)
knowledge_cards.text: No direct lunar or Martian surface combustion data is in PSI yet. PyroZero brackets it using 0g and 1g bounds, ACME E-FIELD electrohydrodynamic ion-wind equivalence, and ZGRF centrifuge scaling ahead of FM2 and LUCI.

knowledge_cards.title: Saffire IV-VI exploration test matrix
knowledge_cards.text: Executed at 20 cm/s flow: SIBAL at 100 kPa/22% O2; cotton jersey at 70.7 kPa/26.2% O2; SIBAL at 54.1 kPa/31.0% O2; two-sided PMMA at 54.6 kPa/30.3% O2 (497 kJ); one-sided PMMA at 55.2 kPa/28.8% O2; Nomex no-ignition at 54.1 kPa/31.9% O2.

knowledge_cards.title: FM2 preliminary lunar flammability result
knowledge_cards.text: The FM2 lab at NASA Glenn reproduces 21% O2 at 14.7 psia and 34% O2 at 8.2 psia. Preliminary centrifuge and drop-tower tests indicate materials have lower limiting oxygen concentrations at Lunar gravity (0.165g) than at 1g.

knowledge_cards.title: 2026 NASA ECLSS Study: 70% Subsystem Material Replacement
knowledge_cards.text: A 2026 NASA ECLSS study (NTRS 20260003925) reported that material flammability is the #1 critical hurdle at 8.2 psia with 34-40% O2, and that roughly 70% of assessed spacecraft subsystems require material replacement.

knowledge_cards.title: July 2026 FDS Fire Model Validated Against Saffire
knowledge_cards.text: A July 2026 NASA paper (ICES-2026-092 / NTRS 20260001600) validated a Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) model against Saffire flight telemetry to predict spacecraft enclosure fire hazards.

knowledge_cards.title: From ISS FLEX research to Fine Water Mist extinguishers
knowledge_cards.text: ISS droplet combustion and suppression research (FLEX) informed the Fine Water Mist Portable Fire Extinguishers (28-46 um droplets) deployed on the ISS to replace toxic Halon/CO2 units.

knowledge_cards.title: Artemis II Orion smoke alarm false-alarm case
knowledge_cards.text: During Artemis II, the crew reported an Orion smoke detector tripping on the second-to-last day (~80,000 miles from Earth). Controllers asked whether it was bumped or triggered by a camera flash; no confirmed cause was established (and not lunar dust as the mission did not land).

knowledge_cards.title: Historical drivers: Apollo 1, Apollo 13, and Mir
knowledge_cards.text: Apollo 1 (1967, 100% O2 at 16.7 psia cabin fire), Apollo 13 (1970, supercritical O2 Tank #2 PTFE wire fire), and Mir (1997, Kvant-1 LiClO4 oxygen candle blowtorch) directly shaped modern prevention, detection, and suppression rules.

knowledge_cards.title: Shared orbital combustion hardware on ISS & Cygnus
knowledge_cards.text: ACME and SoFIE share the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), while FLEX uses the MDCA inside CIR. In the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), BASS, BASS-II, SPICE, and SLICE share the SPICE flow duct, and SAME and DAFT share aerosol instruments. Saffire flew on Cygnus.

knowledge_cards.title: Where NASA PSI data lives (Portal & AWS Open Data)
knowledge_cards.text: NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository is accessible at psi.nasa.gov and mirrored publicly on the AWS Open Data Registry (registry.opendata.aws/nasa-psi).

knowledge_cards.title: Scope boundary: Habitat fires vs. Rocket propellant combustion
knowledge_cards.text: Rocket-engine propellant combustion is out of scope because extreme injector velocities make it independent of gravity. PyroZero focuses strictly on crewed habitats, pressurized rovers, and spacesuit airlocks.
